verdict.summary: LinkedIn provides instant self-serve app registration for basic products like Sign In with LinkedIn and standard scopes, but specialized partner APIs and restricted products require formal review and approval.

evidence.note: Standard consumer auth is self-serve, but specialized developer products require review.

verification.note: Most permissions and partner programs require explicit approval from LinkedIn. Open Permissions are the only permissions that are available to all developers without special approval.

evidence.note: Estimated developer effort to register an app, configure redirect URIs, and implement the OAuth code flow.

steps.title: Register App in Developer Portal
steps.detail: Navigate to the LinkedIn Developer Portal, click Create app, fill out app name, link your verified organization page, and provide logo and privacy policy URLs.
steps.notes: Requires human developer login and organization verification.

evidence.note: App creation steps documented in the authorization code flow guide.

verification.note: Mentions selecting application in Developer Portal and Auth tab, but steps like clicking create app, linking organization page, and privacy policy URLs are missing.

steps.title: Configure Products & Scopes
steps.detail: Go to the Products tab in the developer portal to enable desired products like Sign In with LinkedIn using OpenID Connect or Share on LinkedIn.
steps.notes: Enabling products provisions the required scopes to your app.

evidence.note: Products tab configuration enables relevant scopes.

verification.note: You can apply for new Products under the Products tab.

steps.title: Configure Redirect URIs and Credentials
steps.detail: Navigate to the Auth tab to retrieve your Client ID and Client Secret, and register your absolute HTTPS redirect callback URLs.
steps.notes: Must be absolute HTTPS URIs without URL fragments.

evidence.note: Auth tab stores client credentials and redirect URIs.

verification.note: Click the Auth tab to view your application credentials... Add the redirect (callback) URL via HTTPS to your server.

steps.title: Implement Authorization Code Flow
steps.detail: Implement the 3-legged OAuth code flow in your application, including state parameters and URL-encoded space-delimited scopes.
steps.notes: Can be fully written and tested by an agent using the endpoints.

evidence.note: Endpoints are live and standard OAuth code flow is documented.

verification.note: Follow the steps given below to implement the 3-legged OAuth... scope=liteprofile%20emailaddress%20w_member_social... state=foobar

steps.title: Test Authentication
steps.detail: Test authentication using your own account or the LinkedIn Developer Portal's Token Generator tool.
steps.notes: Requires human browser sign-in for consent screen verification.

evidence.note: Token generator tool provided in the developer portal.

verification.note: The LinkedIn Developer Portal has a token generator for manually creating tokens... If you are using Postman to test this flow...

probes.summary: OpenID Connect discovery document found (issuer: https://www.linkedin.com/oauth).
No RFC 8414 authorization server metadata at 3 candidate location(s).
Authorization endpoint (from docs) responds to a request with a fake client_id (HTTP 200); response mentions an OAuth/client error.
Token endpoint (from docs) is live: an unauthenticated request with a fake code returned OAuth error "invalid_request" (HTTP 400).
Discovery metadata does not advertise a registration_endpoint, so dynamic client registration is likely unsupported.
Metadata does not list code_challenge_methods_supported (PKCE may still be supported; check docs).

limitations: No accounts were created, no forms submitted, no OAuth apps registered, and no credentials were used. Probes are unauthenticated GET requests against public discovery documents, endpoints and documentation pages, plus one unauthenticated POST to the token endpoint with a fake authorization code and a nonexistent client_id (to confirm it answers with an OAuth error).
Review timelines are only marked as sourced when an official provider page states them. Community-reported timelines are labeled as such.
Provider policies change; check the linked sources before relying on a requirement.
